Prepare and export a Seurat object in R

24 November, 2026

Source: vignettes/cerebronexus_workflow_seurat.Rmd
cerebronexus_workflow_seurat.Rmd

Overview

This vignette starts from a Seurat object in which the analysis is already done, adds the tables that CerebroNexus pre-computes (most expressed genes, marker genes, enriched pathways), and exports everything to a .crb file. It does not cover quality control, normalization, clustering or dimensional reduction; for those steps, please see the Seurat tutorials.

These steps are optional: a Seurat object can also be imported as it is, with the Builder or convertSeuratToCerebro(); see From your analysis to an interactive Viewer. The functions shown here take a Seurat object. The same steps, except the gene set enrichment, can also be switched on in the Builder (launchCerebroBuilder()); see Build a data set without writing code.

Installation

Install CerebroNexus as described in the installation instructions. This guide also uses Seurat (install.packages('Seurat')).

Start from a processed Seurat object

CerebroNexus expects an object in which the usual analysis is done:

  • normalized expression values,
  • at least one grouping variable in the meta data, e.g. samples or clusters,
  • at least one dimensional reduction, e.g. UMAP or t-SNE.

Here we use pbmc_small, a processed example of 80 cells and 230 genes that ships with Seurat. It carries clusters, an arbitrary two-level grouping (groups), and PCA and t-SNE coordinates. We copy the clusters to seurat_clusters, the column name Seurat uses in a standard analysis. With your own data, load your object instead and use your own column names.

library(Seurat)
library(CerebroNexus)

data('pbmc_small')
seurat <- UpdateSeuratObject(pbmc_small)
seurat$seurat_clusters <- seurat$RNA_snn_res.1

CerebroNexus functions

Now we use CerebroNexus functions to obtain more information about the data set and its groups. Each function stores its result in the Seurat object, from where the export picks it up.

Calculate percentage of mitochondrial and ribosomal transcripts

First, for every cell we calculate the percentage of mitochondrial and ribosomal transcripts of all transcripts using the addPercentMtRibo() function.

seurat <- addPercentMtRibo(
  seurat,
  organism = 'hg',
  gene_nomenclature = 'name'
)

Get most expressed genes

Another interesting perspective is to look at the 100 most expressed genes for every group. This can help in understanding the transcriptional activity of a given cell population.

seurat <- getMostExpressedGenes(
  seurat,
  assay = 'RNA',
  groups = c('seurat_clusters','groups')
)

Identify marker genes

Marker genes are genes which are particularly strongly or weakly expressed in a given cell population, e.g. a cluster. This information can help to distinguish the role of different cell groups in the data set. We can identify marker genes using the getMarkerGenes() function which internally uses the Seurat::FindAllMarkers() function but also stores the results in the Seurat object under the misc slot.

seurat <- getMarkerGenes(
  seurat,
  assay = 'RNA',
  organism = 'hg',
  groups = c('seurat_clusters','groups'),
  name = 'cerebro_seurat',
  only_pos = TRUE
)

Perform pathway enrichment on marker genes

Using the previously identified marker genes, we can perform a pathway enrichment analysis using the getEnrichedPathways() function. The function will internally use the Enrichr API and store the results in the Seurat object under the misc slot. All we have to do is provide the name that we specified in getMarkerGenes().

seurat <- getEnrichedPathways(
  seurat,
  marker_genes_input = 'cerebro_seurat',
  adj_p_cutoff = 0.01,
  max_terms = 100
)

Gene set enrichment

On top of querying the databases of the Enrichr service, one can also perform gene set enrichment analysis on gene sets provided as a .gmt file, e.g. from the MSigDB. The performGeneSetEnrichmentAnalysis() function uses the GSVA method in combination with additional statistics as published by Diaz-Mejia et al.. It needs the Bioconductor packages GSVA and qvalue:

install.packages('BiocManager')
BiocManager::install(c('GSVA', 'qvalue'))
example_gene_set <- system.file("extdata/example_gene_set.gmt", package = "CerebroNexus")

seurat <- performGeneSetEnrichmentAnalysis(
  seurat,
  assay = 'RNA',
  GMT_file = example_gene_set,
  groups = c('seurat_clusters','groups')
)

Optional extras

Two more kinds of information are exported if the Seurat object carries them.

Cell cycle

If the meta data has a cell cycle column, e.g. Phase from Seurat’s CellCycleScoring() (see the Seurat cell cycle vignette), pass its name to the export with cell_cycle = 'Phase'. The viewer then colours it with its cell cycle palette. The example data has too few cell cycle genes to calculate it here.

3D projections

By default, every dimensional reduction except PCA is exported; one with three dimensions, such as a UMAP computed with n.components = 3, is shown as a 3D projection.

Trajectories (optional)

A Monocle 2 trajectory can be attached to the Seurat object with extractMonocleTrajectory() before the export, and is then shown in the Trajectory tab. See Trajectory analysis for the code.

Export to Cerebro format

Finally, we use CerebroNexus exportFromSeurat() to export our Seurat object to a .crb file which can be loaded into CerebroNexus.

crb_file <- paste0('cerebro_pbmc_seurat_', Sys.Date(), '.crb')

exportFromSeurat(
  seurat,
  assay = 'RNA',
  slot = 'data',
  file = crb_file,
  experiment_name = 'pbmc',
  organism = 'hg',
  groups = c('seurat_clusters','groups'),
  nUMI = 'nCount_RNA',
  nGene = 'nFeature_RNA',
  add_all_meta_data = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

By default the expression matrix is embedded in the .crb. For large data sets, add expression_matrix_mode = "h5" to write the matrix to a sibling .h5 file instead (the only other storage mode); keep the two files together. A very large immune repertoire is moved to a third sibling file (immune_sidecar = "auto"). See Working with large datasets.

Open the result

Open the file in the Viewer:

launchCerebro(crb_file_to_load = crb_file)

The pages Marker genes, Most expressed genes and Enriched pathways show the tables computed above:

The Marker genes page for the exported example. The numbers link the code above to what the page shows.

With this small example, performGeneSetEnrichmentAnalysis() finds no gene set that meets its thresholds, and the Enriched pathways page says so for that method. Tables can be downloaded in CSV or Excel format.

For a direct image export, click Download PNG in the plot toolbar. If the current view supports portable sharing, you can instead open Share view and click Download PNG there. The Share view dialog also lets you download or open a portable JSON configuration containing the current display state and selected cell barcodes, so the same view can be restored in another compatible CerebroNexus session without including the source data.

To share the data set itself, see Share data sets as a Shiny app.

See also

If your Seurat v5 assay is split into one layer per sample, see Seurat v5 layered assays: complete and safe expression matrices for the automatic resolution rules, custom-layer safeguards, and troubleshooting steps.
